special needs schools in the EC

By: Tarryn Crossman | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Special needs schools in the Eastern Cape in a crises

Summary:
There are 46 Government special needs schools in the Eastern Cape and shortage of 2160 places for children

Since 2013 staff at all special needs schools in the Eastern Cape have been fighting for overtime that is due to them, eventually between October last year and March this year staff, from drivers to caretakers, have refused to continue working overtime. Resulting in kids get as little as 3 hours of education a day and being left unattended on the weekends. This has put a spotlight on conditions within special needs schools, but it is just the tip of the ice-burg.
Government Schools for special needs children in the Eastern Cape, especially the boarding schools are in appalling conditions.

We look at three boarding schools that need immediate attention and then take the MEC to board on the bigger picture
The South Africa Nation association for special education – Eastern Cape have an audit of how bad the bigger picture is, staff to children ratio’s, beds to children ratio, living conditions etc.. I am waiting to get this report from them on Wednesday

Further information:
I am working on case studies. Parents who have no option but to send their children to these places, but they know how bad the conditions are or potentially a family that has removed their child?

Timeline: Schools open on the 16th July. I will need to go undercover to the three schools mentioned on the 17th and 18th to see what the conditions are actually like. I also have staff in Vukuhambe who are willing to speak and may be willing to wear spy glasses?

Interviews and confrontations the following week to deliver 5th August

Details on each school are below

East-London – Vukuhamba – HRC are investigating
3 staff for 66 children – woken at 3am to be bathed
No hot water, spodged down
Rooms smelled like urine on my visit
Broken windows
Left alone on Sundays due to overtime disputes
HRC investigating nutritional requirements and expired food.
Mold in all bathroom
Blood all over the male bathroom door when I was there


Mbizana – Sigcau
Boys and girls sleeping in the same quarter. Battling to stop them from procreating
Understaffed
No heating
Matresses on the floor
Old teacher training building that was built in 1970

Grahamstown – Amasango
Old railway house not fit for human inhabitance
Girls and boys together
Understaffed
No running water
Girls and boys housed in the same rooms

Press Release:


Eastern Cape Schools for the Disabled
A Carte Blanche investigation reveals the horror of neglect and poor conditions that children with disabilities face in Eastern Cape government boarding schools. A severe staff shortage in just one school has left 244 children with severe mental and physical disabilities without adequate healthcare and supervision – to fend for themselves, and one another. Why has the Eastern Cape government seemingly turned its back on these extremely vulnerable children?


Script:


Time code CHARACTER / VISUAL
1 00:00 Voice over With limited access to special needs schools. Parents in rural Eastern Cape hand over the primary care for their children to boarding schools. Trusting that their needs will be better met by professionals at home but this couldn’t be further from the truth
2 00:14 Claire Extreme staff shortages, a total lack of staff personal and major structural issues. We investigate government special needs school in the Eastern Cape
3 00:26 Voice over We focused on investigation on 2 boarding schools, IKwezi Lokusa in Mthatha which is school for children with Cerebral Palsy and Othrodepic disabilities and Sigcawu in Bizana which is specifically for children with server intellectual disabilities. Both schools have had staff shortages and infrastructure issues since 2010 which have had dire consequences for the children. We arrived at iKwezi Lokusa on a weekday to find 40 severely disabled children being taken care of by 3 women.

Children lying naked on the freezing floor waiting to be changed, nappies everywhere, the smell of urine,
4 Claire they cannot do anything for themselves. This job requires three women per child not 3 women for 40 children
5 01:18 Nomzukiso At night, we don’t wash them we just wipe them with damp towels here underneath.
6 01:28 Voice over According to school policy the children are supposed to be bathed twice day but housekeeping supervisors like Nomzukiso are over worked due to staff shortages and suffering cares fatigue.
7 01:41 Nomzukiso
I’m trying to do my best because I must be a social worker to them I must be a mother to them, love the as much as possible
8 01:50 Voice over Archie Gulwa has been the principle of IKwezi L since 2010
9 01:56 Claire and Archie Claire: How many housekeeping supervisors should you have and how many do you have at the school?

Archie: we are supposed to be having 48 and we are only having 31

Claire: so, you have 17 vacancies and how long have you had those vacancies

Archie: since 2010
10 02:13 Voice over After working unpaid overtime for years, the house keeping supervisors now refuse and as a result there are no permanent staff on duty between 3 – 6 pm on weekdays
11 02:25 Claire interview with Archie Claire: how many EPWP staff you use between 3 and 6pm

Archie: for the dormitories, we have that is 2 looking after the boys and 2 looking after the girls

Claire: So, you have 4 people looking after 242 children

Archie: Yes, that’s terrible
12 02:40 Voice over On weekends This number is increased to 10 expanded public works staff

13 02:45 Claire and Archie interview Claire: Tell me more about this EPWP staff and how sufficiently are they trained looking after kids with special needs?
Archie: when they come most of them are not well equip for the kids.
Claire: they are learning on the job? With the children here?
Archie: yes
Claire: haven’t there been any incidents? Accidents?
Archie: yeah because you know they bump on each other, push others in wheelchairs and then we have to rush somebody to a nearby clinic because we don’t have a nurse.
14 03:12 Voice over Khwezi Lokusa and Sigcau both base their staff needs on the norms and standards issued by the department in 2013, which requires them to have 2 nurses on site. They have none. Our official tour of IKwezi Lokusa was guided by the deputy principle Mr. Augustine. When we visited the classrooms at 10am we found no teaching staff
15 03:35 Claire and Mr Maphekula Claire: So, 1,2 3, 4,5, 6, 7 learners with no teacher?
Maphekula: There’s supposed to be teacher aids that are here.
Claire: and where are they now?
Maphekula: We have got a shortage when it comes to them.
16 03:51 Claire speaks to camera On the day, they are expecting us we still find rooms full of children with learning disabilities with no supervising adult, teacher or teacher aid.
16 03:58 Voice over There are supposed to 14 teacher Aids at IKwezi Lokusa, but current there are only 5. 5 teacher Aids were put in charge of 114 disabled children
The next classroom also had no teacher

17 04:15 Claire and Maphekula Claire: This is a parent’s worst nightmare. I don’t know if this little girl is on the floor because she has chosen to be there or she fell off the chair.
18 04:26 Voice over While we were in the classroom a teacher aid appeared, he was a previous student. He was previous student at the school
19 04:31 Claire and teacher Claire: Does she climb out by herself?
Teacher: Wheelchair? Yes, she gets in and out by herself
Claire: Does she know how?
Teacher: Yes.
20 04:45 Voice over After telling us the little girl on the floor is able to get in and out of the wheelchair, we watched her battle and fall as she tried to get back into her chair with the help of her teacher aid
21 04:55 Claire and Mr Maphekula Claire: if an emergency happens and people need to evacuate and leave here quickly and nobody was here what was going to happen to her? You do understand my concerns?
Maphekula: I understand your concern
22 05:06 Voice over introduction of Sharon Sharon Maasdorp is the chief Director for education social services at the Department of Education.
23 05:12 Claire and Sharon interview Claire: We visited some government social needs schools in the Eastern Cape, what is the acceptable ratio of the housekeeping supervisors to a special needs child?

Sharon: I’m speaking about the draft guidelines that came out in January. According to that one its 1 to 10

Claire: Are you aware that at IKwezi Lokusa that the ratio between House Supervisor and child is 1 is to 20?
Sharon: I just indicated to you, the draft norms of January 2018 came out to public consumption. We are gradually improving the situation of our
Claire: Gradually is very slow
Sharon: if you must know the backlog of apartheid in our country what it has caused especially in our rural areas and for us as government I can proudly say
Claire: proudly?
Sharon: as Eastern Cape department of education we have achieved so much in changing around the situation. This year we have put 150 non-teaching staff out to improve the situation
Claire: But can you put a timeline to that
Sharon: They will be in place before next year
24 06:18 Voice over Currently at the 46 special needs school in the Eastern Cape there is a non-teaching staff shortage of 513 people. Sigcau is housed in an old teaching training facility that was built in the 1970’s

25 06:32 Claire link It was only supposed to be a temporary structure but 8 years later they are exactly where they started in fact conditions are deteriorating.
26 06:41 Voice over At Sigcau the biggest issue is the proximity of the boys and girl’s dorms, as Children with Severe intellectual disabilities are hypersexualised, they cannot control their sexual impulses and therefore they cannot have this access to each other. We spoke to the HOD Mrs Davies
27 06:58 Claire and Ms David’s Claire: From what age are these children having sex?

Mrs Davids: The kids? The age pf admission here is 10years.
Claire: Are you saying children as young as 10 years could possibly be having sex?
Davids: Not all of them are.
Claire: But possibly we don’t know
Davids: I don’t know
Claire: STI’s, HIV do we know if the children are HIV positive or not?
Davids: Some are HIV positive and they were born HIV Positive the ones I know of
Claire: Have the parents of the children being told that A; there is sexual activity happening at the school and that their child could be at risk of contracting HIV.
Davids: They are not aware. We have been complaining about this condition for time imperious.
28 07:44 Claire and Sharon Claire: The situation at Sigcau is particularly volatile because of the building, are you aware?
Sharon: I’m very much aware
Claire: What are you
Sharon: I’m quit in regular contact with the principle
Claire: how long have you known about that situation there?
Sharon: It could be say a month or 2 ago.
Claire: We were told that you were made of the situation at Sigcawu as early as 2014 and you said you were just told about it 2 months ago?
Sharon: I assume duties on the 3rd of April 2017
Claire: I find it quite unacceptable for you to say I only started in 2017 so I don’t know what was reported to the department in 2014
Sharon: I did not say that, I did not say that. I said I started on the 3rd of April 2017 and that is part of the departments commitment to make sure we turn around the situation.
29 08:37 Voice over Children are assessed by the state and then referred to a special needs school based on this assessment. While at Sigcau we noticed a child, Iviwe, that did not seem to have severe intellectual disabilities. We requested his assessment.
30 08:51 Claire and Davids Claire: From this report, it said ‘t that Iviwe seems to be suffering from a Neurological condition ADHD, they did say that his intellectual function seems to be at a moderate mental retardation. Is Iviwe supposed to be in this school?
Davids: based on that he’s not supposed
31 09:12 Voice over Because there is no occupational therapists or Physiatrists at Sigcau no-one has picked up that Iviwe is intellectually advanced for this school

32 9:19 Claire and Iviwe Claire: What do you want to be when you grow up?
Iviwe: I want to be a doctor.
33 09:26 Voice over Iviwe comes from a remote village near port St Johns, it is a day’s journey from Sigcau. His mother sent him to Sigcau believing it was in his best interests. She trusts the department of education to know what is best for her son

34 09:42 Claire and Nolusindiso Claire: What do you wish for Iviwe in life?
Nolusindiso: Sister as I am talking to you if there was a way for Iviwe to change schools I would be really happy for that. because I would like for him to be in a place that’s good for him so he can reach his full potential.
35 10:05 Claire and Sharon Claire: how many children are in our institutions that should not be
Sharon: Many, many. Even in main stream schools is the biggest challenge. The biggest challenge is in main stream schools. Yes, there are so many that’s why the department is making ta conservative effort to employ now therapists.
36 10:26 Claire and Archie Claire: let’s talk about the vacancies?
Archie: I came here in 2010 and there was not even 1 therapist.
Claire: does the department know this?
Archie: yes, obviously they know it’s not good
37 10:34 Voice over IKwezi Lokusa is supposed to have 3 Social workers, 3 speech therapists, 3 occupational therapists and 3 physiotherapists. None of these posts have ever been filled. in 2017 the department advertised 85 posts for therapist and psychologists, but only 16 of those posts were filled.

38 10:56 Sharon and Claire Sharon: can I just help, what might have happened in some of the cases out of the 85 posts we as head office advertised. Is the fact that physiotherapists, psychologist and OT’s are scarce resources in our country. The second thing also is because it’s a rural area, and your specialist’s proper to go more to the urban areas.
39 11:21 Voice over At the end of the day the ones who are suffering are the children. At IKwezi Lokusa there are 140 children needing physiotherapy. All these children really have are two physio assistants like Hazel

40 11:37 Claire and Nosindiso Claire: when last did she have a session with you?

Nosindiso: We have been dealt with new patients that arrived, it was before school closed.

Claire: So, its maybe 2 months now?
41 11:50 Voice over Independent Cerebral palsy specialists recommended that a child with the least sever CP gets physio once a week


42 11:58 Claire and Nosindiso Claire: the physio itself, is it painful

Nosindiso: To her?

Claire: Yes.

Nosindiso: Yes, sometimes it is especially if they haven’t done it for a while

Sorry, sorry sorry
43 12:12 Sharon and Claire Claire: I feel like the children that have passed through our special needs schools we have failed them. the ones that are at the institution today they will not reap the rewards of all of these programs that you are talking about, we are failing them today!

Sharon: Like I have been failed by the system, I’m a learner with special to make it in the system.
44 12:36 Claire and Archie Claire: if you had a child with CP would you be happy that they came and attended this school

Archie: I would opt for another institution

Claire: that’s heartbreaking

Archie: yeah but that’s the truth

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Special needs schools in the Eastern Cape in a crises
metadata.Summary: There are 46 Government special needs schools in the Eastern Cape and shortage of 2160 places for children Since 2013 staff at all special needs schools in the Eastern Cape have been fighting for overtime that is due to them, eventually between October last year and March this year staff, from drivers to caretakers, have refused to continue working overtime. Resulting in kids get as little as 3 hours of education a day and being left unattended on the weekends. This has put a spotlight on conditions within special needs schools, but it is just the tip of the ice-burg. Government Schools for special needs children in the Eastern Cape, especially the boarding schools are in appalling conditions. We look at three boarding schools that need immediate attention and then take the MEC to board on the bigger picture The South Africa Nation association for special education – Eastern Cape have an audit of how bad the bigger picture is, staff to children ratio’s, beds to children ratio, living conditions etc.. I am waiting to get this report from them on Wednesday
metadata.Further information: I am working on case studies. Parents who have no option but to send their children to these places, but they know how bad the conditions are or potentially a family that has removed their child? Timeline: Schools open on the 16th July. I will need to go undercover to the three schools mentioned on the 17th and 18th to see what the conditions are actually like. I also have staff in Vukuhambe who are willing to speak and may be willing to wear spy glasses? Interviews and confrontations the following week to deliver 5th August Details on each school are below East-London – Vukuhamba – HRC are investigating 3 staff for 66 children – woken at 3am to be bathed No hot water, spodged down Rooms smelled like urine on my visit Broken windows Left alone on Sundays due to overtime disputes HRC investigating nutritional requirements and expired food. Mold in all bathroom Blood all over the male bathroom door when I was there Mbizana – Sigcau Boys and girls sleeping in the same quarter. Battling to stop them from procreating Understaffed No heating Matresses on the floor Old teacher training building that was built in 1970 Grahamstown – Amasango Old railway house not fit for human inhabitance Girls and boys together Understaffed No running water Girls and boys housed in the same rooms
